title: Finding Longitude at Sea
text:
For centuries, sailors could find their latitude, their position north or south, fairly easily by measuring the height of the Sun or certain stars. Longitude, their position east or west, was a much harder problem. Because the Earth turns 15 degrees every hour, a ship's longitude could be calculated by comparing local time with the time at a home port, but only if the ship carried a clock that kept accurate time for months on a moving, wet ship with changing temperatures. No such clock existed.

The consequences were serious. Ships lost their way, voyages took longer than necessary and many ships were wrecked. In 1707, a British fleet ran onto rocks near the Isles of Scilly, and around 1,500 sailors died. In 1714, the British Parliament passed the Longitude Act, offering a large prize for a practical method of finding longitude at sea.

Many astronomers believed that the answer would come from observing the Moon's position among the stars. John Harrison, a carpenter and self-taught clockmaker, chose a different path. Over several decades, he built a series of marine timekeepers. His fourth, completed in 1759 and not much larger than a big pocket watch, lost only about five seconds on a voyage to Jamaica lasting more than two months. Nevertheless, the Board of Longitude was slow to give him the full reward, partly because some members preferred the astronomical method. Harrison finally received a large sum in 1773, after the King himself supported his case.

questions.q: According to the passage, a ship's longitude could be calculated if ----.
options: sailors measured the height of the Sun or of certain stars very carefully
the Earth turned more slowly
the ship carried a clock showing the accurate time at its home port
the Moon's position were ignored
the ship sailed only north or south
questions.explain: Metin 'only if the ship carried a clock that kept accurate time' diyor ve karşılaştırma ana limanın saatiyle. Şık bunu 'clock showing the accurate time at its home port' ile veriyor.
questions.anlam: Soru: Bir geminin boylamı hangi koşulda hesaplanabilirdi? Dayanak (1. paragraf): 'Yerel saat ana limandaki saatle karşılaştırılarak, ama sadece gemi aylarca doğru çalışan bir saat taşırsa.'

Kuzey-güney hareket enlemle ilgili; boylam sorununu çözmez.

why: Metinle çelişiyor: dördüncü saat sadece yaklaşık beş saniye kaybetti.
Harrison astronom olmadı; marangoz ve saatçiydi.

Ters bilgi: Kral onu destekledi.

title: Under the River
text:
When construction of the Brooklyn Bridge began in 1870, the foundations of its two towers had to rest on firm material beneath the bed of the East River, which necessitated the use of caissons, enormous timber boxes, open at the bottom, that were sunk onto the river floor. Compressed air pumped into the working chamber kept out water and mud, allowing labourers to excavate the bed beneath them, whereupon the caisson, weighted with the growing masonry tower above, descended gradually.

The deeper the caisson sank, the higher the air pressure required, and with it came a mysterious affliction. Workers who returned to the surface after a shift experienced severe joint pain, paralysis and in some cases death; because sufferers were often bent over in agony, the condition was dubbed 'the bends'. It is now understood that, under pressure, nitrogen dissolves in the blood and tissues in greater quantities, and that if the pressure is reduced too rapidly, it forms bubbles, much as carbon dioxide does when a bottle of soda is opened. Gradual decompression, which allows the gas to escape harmlessly through the lungs, was not then standard practice.

The chief engineer, Washington Roebling, who had taken over the project after his father John died of tetanus following an accident, was himself disabled by the condition. Confined to his room overlooking the site, he directed the remainder of the work by observing through a telescope and dictating instructions to his wife, Emily Warren Roebling, who acquired considerable engineering knowledge and served as the indispensable intermediary between him and the engineers. Notably, when the Manhattan caisson reached a depth of about 24 metres without encountering bedrock, Roebling halted it there, judging that the risk to the workers outweighed that of founding the tower on compacted sand.

options: Building a Bridge at a Human Cost
How Soda Bottles Inspired Bridge Design
Why Bedrock Is Unnecessary for Bridges
The Life of John Roebling

questions.explain: Metin köprü yapımını, işçilerdeki vurgun hastalığını ve Roebling'in sakat kalmasını anlatıyor. 'Building a Bridge at a Human Cost' bunu kapsıyor.

Teleskop sadece Roebling'in işi izleme aracı.

why: Kulenin çöktüğü metinde yazmıyor.

title: Ships That Snapped
text:
During the Second World War, American shipyards produced some 2,700 Liberty ships, cargo vessels whose hulls were, unusually for the period, assembled almost entirely by welding rather than riveting. Welding saved time and steel, enabling a ship to be completed in weeks, yet it also eliminated the riveted joints that in conventional hulls had acted as natural crack arresters. In a welded hull, a crack originating at one point could propagate continuously through the plating.

Within a few years, hundreds of the ships had developed serious fractures, and a small number broke completely in two. The investigations that followed identified several contributing factors. Many fractures originated at square hatch corners, where stresses were concentrated, and at defective welds. Most significantly, the steel used, although adequate in strength, became brittle at low temperatures; failures were markedly more frequent in the cold waters of the North Atlantic, where the plates were below their ductile-to-brittle transition temperature, the temperature below which a steel fractures with little absorption of energy.

The episode had a profound influence on engineering practice. Constance Tipper, a metallurgist at the University of Cambridge, demonstrated that the transition depended on the steel rather than on the welding alone, and impact tests such as the Charpy test, in which a notched specimen is struck by a pendulum, came to be specified routinely for structural steels. Hatch corners were redesigned with rounded shapes, and the episode contributed to the development of fracture mechanics, the discipline which accepts that structures contain flaws and asks under what conditions those flaws will grow.

questions.q: According to the passage, welding contributed to the failures because ----.
options: it was used only at hatch corners
it removed joints that had previously stopped cracks from spreading
it made ships take years to complete
it raised the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature of the steel plates
it used more steel than riveting did
questions.explain: Metin 'eliminated the riveted joints that ... had acted as natural crack arresters' diyor. Şık 'eliminated' yerine 'removed', 'crack arresters' yerine 'stopped cracks from spreading' kullanıyor.
questions.anlam: Soru: Kaynak hasarlara nasıl katkıda bulundu? Dayanak (1. paragraf): 'Kaynak, geleneksel gövdelerde doğal çatlak durdurucu olan perçinli birleşimleri ortadan kaldırdı.'
why: Metinle çelişiyor: gövdeler neredeyse tamamen kaynakla birleştirildi.
Metinle çelişiyor: kaynak gemiyi haftalar içinde bitirmeyi sağladı.
Geçiş sıcaklığı çeliğe bağlıydı; kaynağın yükselttiği yazmıyor.
Metinle çelişiyor: kaynak çelik tasarrufu sağladı.
questions.tip: 'yet it also' kalıbı bir faydanın ardından gelen zararı verir; cevap 'yet' sonrasındadır.

questions.q: It can be inferred from the passage that a Liberty ship ----.
options: would have been completely immune to fracture if its steel had been stronger
fractured with high energy absorption in cold water
could break only while it was moored in port
was more likely to fracture in the North Atlantic than in warmer waters
would not have needed impact testing if it had been riveted

questions.anlam: Soru: Bir Liberty gemisi hakkında ne çıkarılabilir? Dayanak (2. paragraf): 'Hasarlar Kuzey Atlantik'in soğuk sularında belirgin şekilde daha sıktı.'
why: Metinle çelişiyor: çeliğin mukavemeti yeterliydi; sorun düşük sıcaklıkta gevreklik.
Ters bilgi: geçiş sıcaklığının altında çelik az enerji soğurarak kırılır.

title: Bees That Dance Directions
text:
When a honeybee forager discovers a rich patch of flowers, it returns to the hive and performs a series of movements on the vertical surface of the comb. This behaviour, known as the waggle dance, was decoded in the 1940s by the Austrian zoologist Karl von Frisch, who later shared a Nobel Prize for his work.

During the dance, the bee runs forward in a straight line while shaking its abdomen from side to side, then circles back and repeats the run. The angle of the straight run relative to vertical corresponds to the angle between the food source and the sun, as seen from the hive. The duration of the waggle phase, meanwhile, indicates distance: the longer the bee waggles, the farther away the flowers are.

Because the hive is dark, other workers follow the dancer closely and detect its movements largely through touch and vibrations. They also sample the scent of the flowers carried on its body. Remarkably, bees adjust the angle of their dance over the course of the day to compensate for the movement of the sun, which suggests that they possess an internal sense of time.

options: shows the angle between the flowers and the sun as seen from the hive

is detected by the other workers mainly through their sense of sight

title: Crows That Make Hooks
text:
Tool use was once regarded as a defining feature of humans, but it has since been documented in a wide range of animals. Among the most sophisticated tool users are New Caledonian crows, which inhabit a group of islands in the South Pacific. These birds fashion hooks from twigs by stripping away leaves and carefully shaping the end, and they cut stepped tools from the stiff edges of pandanus leaves. Such tools are used to extract insect larvae from holes in dead wood, a food source that would otherwise be largely inaccessible.

What distinguishes these crows is not merely that they use tools but that the design of their tools varies from one region to another. Since these differences do not appear to reflect local differences in available materials, some researchers interpret them as a form of cultural transmission, in which young birds acquire techniques by observing older ones. Supporting this view, juveniles raised in captivity without adult models do attempt to use sticks, yet their tools are considerably cruder. Thus, although a basic tendency to manipulate objects seems to be inherited, refinement appears to depend on social learning.

questions.q: According to the passage, New Caledonian crows use their tools mainly to ----.

strip the leaves from twigs in order to feed their young

obtain insect larvae hidden in holes in dead wood
questions.explain: Metin 'used to extract insect larvae from holes in dead wood' diyor. Şık 'extract' yerine 'obtain', 'holes' bilgisini 'hidden in holes' ile veriyor.
questions.anlam: Soru: Yeni Kaledonya kargaları aletlerini esas olarak ne için kullanır? Dayanak (1. paragraf): 'Bu aletler ölü ağaçtaki deliklerden böcek larvalarını çıkarmak için kullanılır.'

title: Finding the Way South
text:
Every autumn, billions of songbirds leave their breeding grounds and fly thousands of kilometres to wintering areas, often travelling alone and at night. Many young birds complete this journey without ever having made it before, which shows that at least part of the route information is inherited.

To stay on course, birds appear to use several compasses. During the day, they can orient themselves by the position of the sun, correcting for its movement across the sky. At night, many species use the pattern of stars around the celestial pole; experiments in planetariums have shown that birds raised under an artificial sky learn to orient by whichever point the stars rotate around. In addition, birds can sense the Earth's magnetic field, even when the sky is cloudy.

How the magnetic sense works is still debated. One leading hypothesis proposes that light-sensitive molecules in the eye undergo chemical reactions influenced by the magnetic field, so that birds may literally see magnetic lines. Interestingly, experienced adults that are moved to a new location by researchers can correct their route, whereas young birds usually continue in the inherited direction and miss their goal.

title: Roads Made of Scent
text:
Ants are tiny and nearly blind, yet a colony can find food quickly and organise thousands of workers without any leader. One of the main tools they use is chemical communication.

When a worker ant finds food, it returns to the nest and leaves a trail of a chemical called a pheromone on the ground. Other ants smell the trail and follow it to the food. When they come back, they add more pheromone, so the trail becomes stronger. If the food runs out, the ants stop marking the path, and the scent slowly disappears.

This simple system has a clever result. Suppose there are two paths to the same food, one short and one long. Ants using the short path finish each trip faster, so they add pheromone to it more often. Soon the short path smells stronger, and most ants choose it. In this way, the colony finds the best route, although no single ant compares the two paths.

Computer scientists have copied this idea. Programs based on the behaviour of ant colonies are now used to plan routes for delivery trucks and to send data through computer networks.

title: Nets Made of Bubbles
text:
Humpback whales, despite their enormous size, feed largely on small prey such as krill and schooling fish, and some populations have developed a striking method of concentrating them. In bubble-net feeding, one or more whales dive beneath a school and swim upwards in a spiral while releasing air from their blowholes. The rising bubbles form a cylindrical curtain that the fish are reluctant to cross, so the school is compressed into a tight mass near the surface. The whales then lunge upwards through the centre with their mouths wide open, engulfing a large portion of the prey in a single gulp.

In south-east Alaska, groups of whales have been observed coordinating this behaviour, with particular individuals apparently taking specific roles: one blows the bubbles, while others produce loud calls that may help to drive the fish together. Such groups sometimes remain stable over several years. Elsewhere, humpbacks employ different techniques, including slapping the water with their tails before releasing bubbles, a variant that spread through one population within a few decades. Its rapid spread, far too fast to be explained by genetic change, is regarded as evidence of social learning.

breaks the school of fish into several smaller groups

title: Learning to Sing
text:
Many songbirds are not born knowing their songs. In species such as the zebra finch, a young male must learn to sing by listening to an adult, usually his father, in a process that resembles the way human infants learn to speak.

Learning takes place in two stages. First, during a sensitive period early in life, the young bird listens and forms a memory of the adult song, even though he does not yet sing it himself. Later, he begins to produce quiet, unstructured sounds, which are often compared to the babbling of babies. By practising and comparing his own output with the stored memory, he gradually improves until his song closely matches the model. If a young bird is raised in isolation, he still sings, but his song is simple and abnormal.

Hearing is essential throughout this process. Birds that are deafened after memorising a song but before practising it fail to develop a normal song, because they cannot compare what they produce with what they remember. For these reasons, songbirds have become important models for studying how the brain learns complex sequences of sounds, including speech.

questions.q: According to the passage, during the sensitive period, a young zebra finch ----.
options: forms a memory of the adult song without singing it yet
produces quiet sounds similar to the babbling of babies
compares his own song carefully with the song that his father sings
teaches the song he has learned to other young males
gradually loses his ability to hear adult songs
questions.explain: Metin 'forms a memory of the adult song, even though he does not yet sing it himself' diyor. Şık bunu 'without singing it yet' ile veriyor.
questions.anlam: Soru: Hassas dönemde genç zebra ispinozu ne yapar? Dayanak (2. paragraf): 'Genç kuş dinler ve yetişkin şarkısının hafızasını oluşturur, ama henüz kendisi söylemez.'
why: Sessiz sesler ikinci aşamada (Later) gelir.
Karşılaştırma pratik aşamasında yapılır; hassas dönemde değil.

title: Words for Danger
text:
Vervet monkeys live in groups in the grasslands and forests of eastern and southern Africa. They are hunted by several kinds of predators, and they have developed different alarm calls for different dangers.

When a monkey sees a leopard, it gives a loud barking call. The other monkeys then run up into the trees, where the leopard cannot easily follow them. When an eagle appears, a different, coughing call is given, and the monkeys look up and hide in bushes. A third call warns of snakes; on hearing it, the monkeys stand up on their back legs and look carefully at the ground around them.

In the 1970s, researchers tested these calls by hiding a loudspeaker and playing recorded calls when no predator was present. The monkeys still reacted in the correct way for each call. This showed that the sound alone, and not the sight of the predator, carried the information.

Young vervets are not perfect at first. They sometimes give eagle calls for harmless birds, such as pigeons. With experience, however, they learn to call only for real threats.

questions.q: According to the passage, when vervet monkeys hear the snake call, they ----.
options: run up into the trees to escape quickly
stand up and look carefully at the ground
look up at the sky and hide in bushes
give a loud barking call to the rest of the group
move to open grassland, where snakes are easier to see
questions.explain: Metin 'stand up on their back legs and look carefully at the ground' diyor. Şık bunu kısaltarak 'stand up and look carefully at the ground' diye veriyor.
questions.anlam: Soru: Yılan çağrısını duyan maymunlar ne yapar? Dayanak (2. paragraf): 'Arka ayakları üzerinde dikilir ve çevrelerindeki yere dikkatle bakarlar.'

Bu kartal çağrısının tepkisi.

why: Metinle çelişiyor: avcıyı görmeden de doğru tepki verdiler.

title: Plants That Feed the Soil
text:
Plants need nitrogen to grow, and farmers often add it to their fields as chemical fertiliser. Producing this fertiliser, however, uses a lot of energy, and when too much is applied, the extra nitrogen can wash into rivers and harm the life in them. For this reason, many farmers also use an old and natural method: they grow legumes.

Legumes are plants such as beans, peas, lentils and clover. On their roots, they have small swellings called nodules. Inside these nodules live bacteria that can take nitrogen gas from the air and change it into a form that plants can use. The plant gives the bacteria sugar, and in return the bacteria supply nitrogen.

When a legume crop is harvested, its roots and other leftover parts stay in the soil and slowly break down. The nitrogen they contain then becomes available to the next crop. This is one reason why farmers rotate crops, for example by growing wheat in a field one year and beans the next. Crop rotation also helps to reduce pests and diseases, because many of them attack only one type of plant.

questions.q: According to the passage, the bacteria in root nodules ----.
options: change nitrogen gas from the air into a usable form
give sugar to the plant in return for nitrogen
wash the extra nitrogen into nearby rivers
attack only one type of plant, such as wheat
are added to fields as a kind of chemical fertiliser
questions.explain: Metin 'take nitrogen gas from the air and change it into a form that plants can use' diyor. Şık 'a form that plants can use' yerine 'a usable form' kullanıyor.
questions.anlam: Soru: Kök nodüllerindeki bakteriler ne yapar? Dayanak (2. paragraf): 'Bu bakteriler havadaki azot gazını alıp bitkinin kullanabileceği bir biçime çevirir.'
why: Rolleri ters çeviriyor: şekeri bitki verir, azotu bakteri.

Tek tür bitkiye saldırmak zararlıların özelliği.
Bakteriler kimyasal gübre değil, doğal bir yöntemin parçası.
questions.tip: Karşılıklı alışverişte ('gives ..., in return ...') kimin neyi verdiğini dikkatle eşle.

questions.q: The passage mentions that crop rotation reduces pests and diseases because ----.

title: Water Drop by Drop
text:
Agriculture accounts for roughly 70 percent of the fresh water withdrawn by humans, and in many dry regions the supply is already under severe pressure. Traditional flood irrigation, in which water is allowed to flow across the surface of a field, is cheap and simple, but much of the water evaporates or drains below the reach of the roots before plants can use it.

Drip irrigation offers an alternative. Water is delivered through a network of plastic pipes and released slowly, drop by drop, from small openings called emitters placed close to each plant. Because the water goes directly to the root zone, losses are greatly reduced, and farmers can often grow the same crop with considerably less water. Fertiliser can also be dissolved in the water and supplied in precise amounts, a practice known as fertigation.

The method has drawbacks, however. Installation is expensive, which puts it out of reach for many small farmers unless subsidies are available. Emitters can become blocked by sediment or mineral deposits, so the water often needs filtering. Moreover, studies have shown that saving water on each field does not always reduce total use in a region, since farmers may expand the irrigated area.

questions.q: According to the passage, flood irrigation wastes water because ----.
options: it requires an expensive network of plastic pipes
much of it evaporates or drains too deep before roots can use it
its emitters are often blocked by mineral deposits
the fertiliser dissolved in it must first be filtered to remove sediment
it is used only in regions with plenty of rainfall
questions.explain: Metin 'much of the water evaporates or drains below the reach of the roots' diyor. Şık 'below the reach of the roots' yerine 'drains too deep' kullanıyor.
questions.anlam: Soru: Salma sulama suyu neden boşa harcar? Dayanak (1. paragraf): 'Suyun çoğu bitkiler kullanamadan buharlaşır ya da köklerin ulaşamadığı derinliğe süzülür.'
why: Plastik boru ağı damla sulamaya ait; iki yöntemi karıştırıyor.
Damlatıcılar damla sulamaya ait.
Suya gübre katmak damla sulamada (fertigation) olur.
Metinde salma sulamanın sadece yağışlı bölgelerde kullanıldığı yazmıyor.
questions.tip: İki yöntem anlatılıyorsa sorudaki yöntemin paragrafında kal; diğerinin parçaları tuzaktır.

reduces the cost of installing a drip system

questions.anlam: Soru: Fertigasyon nedir? Dayanak (2. paragraf): 'Gübre suda çözülüp hassas miktarlarda verilebilir; buna fertigasyon denir.'
why: Tıkanan damlatıcıyı temizlemek filtreleme ile ilgili; fertigasyon değil.

title: Why Bread Goes Stale
text:
It is commonly assumed that bread becomes stale because it dries out, yet bread sealed in an airtight bag still hardens within a few days, and stale bread may contain nearly as much water as fresh bread. The principal cause, in fact, lies in changes to starch, the main component of flour.

In raw flour, starch exists as tightly packed granules with a partly crystalline structure. During baking, these granules absorb water and swell, and the long starch molecules lose their ordered arrangement; this process, known as gelatinisation, gives fresh bread its soft texture. Once the loaf cools, however, the molecules gradually begin to realign and form crystalline regions again, a process termed retrogradation. As they do so, water is expelled from the starch and moves into other parts of the crumb, which consequently becomes firm and crumbly.

Retrogradation proceeds fastest at temperatures just above freezing, which explains why bread kept in a refrigerator tends to stale more rapidly than bread kept at room temperature. Freezing, by contrast, slows the process almost to a halt. Gentle reheating can temporarily reverse staling, though the effect is short-lived.

questions.q: According to the passage, gelatinisation ----.
options: occurs during baking as starch granules take up water and swell
causes water to be expelled from the starch after cooling
is the main reason why bread dries out in an airtight bag
makes the starch molecules form crystalline regions again
takes place most quickly at temperatures just above the freezing point
questions.explain: Metin 'During baking, these granules absorb water and swell' diyor. Şık 'absorb' yerine 'take up' kullanıyor.
questions.anlam: Soru: Jelatinleşme nedir? Dayanak (2. paragraf): 'Pişirme sırasında granüller su emer ve şişer, molekül düzeni bozulur; buna jelatinleşme denir.'
why: Suyun dışarı atılması soğumadan sonra, retrogradasyonda olur.
Metinle çelişiyor: bayatlamanın ana sebebi kuruma değil nişasta değişimi.
Kristal bölgelerin yeniden oluşması retrogradasyon; iki süreci karıştırıyor.
Donma noktasının hemen üstünde hızlanan süreç retrogradasyon.
questions.tip: Birbirine zıt iki süreç varsa (jelatinleşme / retrogradasyon) her şıkkın hangisine ait olduğunu işaretle.

questions.q: It is stated in the passage that, during retrogradation, ----.

the crumb of the loaf becomes softer as it cools
questions.explain: Metin 'water is expelled from the starch and moves into other parts of the crumb' diyor. Şık 'is expelled' yerine 'leaves' kullanıyor.
questions.anlam: Soru: Retrogradasyon sırasında ne olur? Dayanak (2. paragraf): 'Su nişastadan atılır ve ekmek içinin diğer kısımlarına geçer.'

Metinle çelişiyor: bayat ekmekte su neredeyse aynı miktarda kalır.

questions.tip: Soruda 'during X' varsa metinde X'in adının geçtiği cümlenin hemen sonrasını oku.

title: Enemies of the Enemy
text:
Chemical pesticides have helped to raise crop yields, but their heavy use has brought problems. Many pests have become resistant, and the chemicals can kill beneficial insects, such as pollinators and the natural enemies of the pests themselves. One response to these problems is biological control, the use of living organisms to suppress pest populations.

A well-known early example comes from California in the 1880s, when an insect called the cottony cushion scale threatened to destroy the state's citrus industry. A ladybird beetle was brought from Australia, where the scale had originated, and within a few years the pest was largely under control. Today, greenhouse growers routinely release tiny parasitic wasps, which lay their eggs inside whiteflies; the developing wasp larvae kill their hosts.

Biological control is not free of risk, however. Introduced species have sometimes attacked native organisms instead of the intended pest. The cane toad, released in Australia in the 1930s to control beetles in sugar cane, failed to do so and became a serious pest itself. For this reason, candidate species are now tested carefully, often for years, to make sure that they feed only on their target before they are released.

questions.q: According to the passage, the ladybird beetle brought to California ----.
options: attacked native organisms instead of the cottony cushion scale
laid its eggs inside whiteflies in citrus greenhouses
was tested for several years before it was released
was resistant to the chemical pesticides used on citrus

questions.explain: Metin böceğin 'from Australia, where the scale had originated' getirildiğini söylüyor. Şık bunu 'came from the same region as the scale insect' diye veriyor.
questions.anlam: Soru: Kaliforniya'ya getirilen uğur böceği hakkında ne söyleniyor? Dayanak (2. paragraf): 'Uğur böceği, pamuklu koşnilin kökeni olan Avustralya'dan getirildi.'
why: Yerli canlılara saldıran örnek kara kurbağası; uğur böceği zararlıyı kontrol etti.
Beyaz sineğe yumurta bırakan parazit eşek arıları.

Pestisit direnci uğur böceği için söylenmiyor.
questions.tip: 'where' ile başlayan yan cümle bir yer hakkında ek bilgi verir; bu tür ekler sık sık cevap olur.

questions.q: The passage mentions that the parasitic wasps used in greenhouses ----.

questions.anlam: Soru: Seralardaki parazit eşek arıları hakkında ne söyleniyor? Dayanak (2. paragraf): 'Yumurtalarını beyaz sineklerin içine bırakırlar; gelişen larvalar konaklarını öldürür.'
why: Bitkilerle beslendikleri yazmıyor.

title: The Daily Sea Breeze
text:
People who live on coasts are familiar with a cool wind that often blows from the sea on sunny afternoons. This sea breeze results from the fact that land and water heat up at different rates.

Water has a high heat capacity, which means that it must absorb a large amount of energy to raise its temperature. In addition, sunlight penetrates some distance into the sea, and waves and currents mix the warmed surface water with cooler water below. Land, by contrast, heats quickly because the energy is concentrated in a thin surface layer. As a result, by late morning the air above the land becomes warmer than the air above the sea. The warm air expands and rises, lowering the pressure near the ground, and cooler, denser air from the sea flows in to replace it.

At night, the pattern is reversed. The land loses heat more quickly than the water, so the air over the sea becomes relatively warm, and a weaker land breeze blows offshore. Sea breezes can bring welcome relief during hot weather, and where the incoming air meets rising air inland, they can also trigger afternoon thunderstorms.

questions.q: According to the passage, land heats up more quickly than the sea because ----.
options: it has a higher heat capacity than water does
sunlight penetrates more deeply into soil than into water
waves and currents mix warm air with the cooler air above
the energy it absorbs stays in a thin surface layer
the air above it is cooler and denser in the morning
questions.explain: Metin 'Land ... heats quickly because the energy is concentrated in a thin surface layer' diyor. Şık 'concentrated' yerine 'stays' kullanıyor.
questions.anlam: Soru: Kara neden denizden daha hızlı ısınır? Dayanak (2. paragraf): 'Kara hızlı ısınır çünkü enerji ince bir yüzey katmanında toplanır.'
why: Isı kapasitesi yüksek olan sudur; kara değil.

title: Ice from a Summer Sky
text:
Hail, paradoxically, is most common in late spring and summer, when surface temperatures are high. This is because hailstones form only within cumulonimbus clouds containing powerful updrafts, and such updrafts are fuelled by warm, moist air rising from a heated surface.

A hailstone begins as a small embryo, often a frozen raindrop or a pellet of soft ice, carried upwards into a region of the cloud where the temperature is well below freezing. There, it collides with supercooled water droplets, which remain liquid despite the low temperature but freeze on contact with a solid surface. Where droplets are sparse and freeze instantly, they trap tiny air bubbles and produce cloudy ice; where they are abundant, the water spreads over the stone before freezing, forming clear ice. The alternating layers visible when a hailstone is cut open therefore record the varying conditions it has passed through, rather than, as was once believed, a corresponding number of trips up and down the cloud.

A stone continues to grow for as long as the updraft can support its weight. Updrafts exceeding 160 kilometres per hour are required to hold stones the size of a tennis ball, which can severely damage crops, vehicles and roofs.

questions.q: According to the passage, supercooled water droplets ----.
options: form the frozen embryo at the centre of every hailstone
are carried upwards only by updrafts faster than 160 km per hour
stay liquid below freezing but freeze when they touch a solid
trap the air bubbles that make a hailstone transparent
are most common near a heated surface during summer
questions.explain: Metin 'remain liquid despite the low temperature but freeze on contact with a solid surface' diyor. Şık 'despite the low temperature' yerine 'below freezing' kullanıyor.
questions.anlam: Soru: Aşırı soğumuş su damlacıkları hakkında ne söyleniyor? Dayanak (2. paragraf): 'Düşük sıcaklığa rağmen sıvı kalırlar ama katı bir yüzeye değince donarlar.'
why: Embriyo donmuş yağmur damlası ya da yumuşak buzdur; aşırı soğumuş damla değil.

Ters bilgi: hava kabarcıkları buzu bulanık yapar, şeffaf değil.
Damlacıklar bulutun donma noktası altındaki bölgesinde; yüzeyde değil.

questions.anlam: Soru: Şeffaf buz ne zaman oluşur? Dayanak (2. paragraf): 'Damlacıklar bol olduğunda su donmadan önce taşın üzerine yayılır ve şeffaf buz oluşur.'

title: Rivers of Wind
text:
Several kilometres above the Earth's surface, narrow bands of strong wind flow from west to east around the globe. These jet streams, which can reach speeds of more than 300 kilometres per hour, form along boundaries where air masses of very different temperatures meet. The polar front jet, which separates cold polar air from warmer air to the south, is the most influential for weather in the middle latitudes.

The jet stream rarely flows in a straight line. Instead, it meanders in large waves, and the low- and high-pressure systems that bring changeable weather to Europe and North America tend to develop and travel along its path. Airlines also take it into account: eastbound transatlantic flights are often considerably shorter than westbound ones because aircraft can ride the jet.

Occasionally, the waves become greatly amplified and almost stationary, a situation described as blocking. Weather patterns then persist over the same region for days or weeks, potentially producing prolonged heatwaves, droughts or floods. Some researchers have argued that rapid warming of the Arctic, by reducing the temperature contrast that drives the jet, may make such patterns more frequent; others contend that the evidence remains inconclusive, partly because natural variability in the jet is large.

questions.q: According to the passage, jet streams form ----.

when aircraft fly eastwards across the Atlantic

questions.anlam: Soru: Jet akımları nerede oluşur? Dayanak (1. paragraf): 'Sıcaklıkları çok farklı hava kütlelerinin buluştuğu sınırlar boyunca oluşurlar.'

title: Food for Our Microbes
text:
The human large intestine is home to trillions of bacteria, collectively known as the gut microbiota. Many of these microbes depend on a part of our diet that we ourselves cannot digest: dietary fibre, found in vegetables, fruit, whole grains and legumes.

Because human enzymes cannot break fibre down, it passes through the small intestine largely unchanged. In the colon, however, bacteria ferment it and produce short-chain fatty acids, such as butyrate. Butyrate serves as the main energy source for the cells lining the colon, and it appears to help maintain the barrier that prevents harmful substances from passing from the gut into the blood. These fatty acids may also reduce inflammation.

Diets in many industrialised countries contain far less fibre than is recommended. In experiments with mice, low-fibre diets reduced the diversity of gut bacteria, and some microbes began to feed on the protective mucus layer of the intestine instead. Moreover, when such diets continued over several generations, some bacterial species disappeared and did not return even after fibre was added again. Although results from mice cannot be applied directly to humans, they suggest that long-term dietary habits may shape the microbiota in lasting ways.

title: Cooling Down
text:
The human body works best at a core temperature of about 37 °C. When we exercise or the weather is hot, the body produces or gains extra heat, and it must lose this heat to stay healthy. The most important way it does this is by sweating.

Our skin contains millions of sweat glands. When the brain detects that the body is getting too warm, it sends signals to these glands, and they release a salty liquid onto the skin. The sweat itself does not cool us. Cooling happens when the sweat evaporates, because evaporation takes heat from the skin.

For this reason, sweating works well in dry air but poorly in humid air. When the air already contains a lot of water vapour, sweat evaporates slowly and simply runs off the body. This is why a hot, humid day can feel more uncomfortable, and be more dangerous, than a hotter but drier one.

During long exercise in the heat, a person can lose more than a litre of sweat per hour. If this water and salt are not replaced, the person may become dehydrated, and the body's cooling system can start to fail.

questions.q: According to the passage, the body is cooled when ----.

questions.explain: Metin 'Cooling happens when the sweat evaporates, because evaporation takes heat from the skin' diyor. Şık 'takes heat from the skin' yerine 'takes heat away' kullanıyor.
questions.anlam: Soru: Vücut ne zaman serinler? Dayanak (2. paragraf): 'Ter kendisi serinletmez; serinleme ter buharlaştığında olur, çünkü buharlaşma deriden ısı alır.'

Beyin sinyal gönderince ter salınır; durdurmak serinletmez.

title: Breathing Thin Air
text:
At an altitude of 4,000 metres, each breath contains roughly 40 percent less oxygen than at sea level, because the air pressure is lower, although the proportion of oxygen in the air remains the same. Lowlanders who ascend rapidly to such heights often experience headaches, nausea and fatigue, and in severe cases fluid may accumulate in the lungs or brain.

Over days and weeks, the body acclimatises. Breathing becomes deeper and faster, and the kidneys release a hormone called erythropoietin, which stimulates the production of red blood cells and so increases the blood's capacity to carry oxygen. This response, however, has a cost: blood containing too many red cells becomes thicker, placing additional strain on the heart.

Populations that have lived at high altitude for thousands of years have adapted in different ways. Many Andean highlanders have relatively high haemoglobin concentrations, whereas Tibetans typically maintain concentrations close to those of lowlanders and instead compensate partly through increased breathing and blood flow. Genetic studies have linked the Tibetan pattern to a variant of a gene called EPAS1, which is involved in the body's response to low oxygen; strikingly, this variant appears to have been inherited from Denisovans, an extinct group of archaic humans.

questions.explain: Metin 'because the air pressure is lower, although the proportion of oxygen in the air remains the same' diyor. Şık sebep kısmını veriyor.
questions.anlam: Soru: 4.000 metrede her nefeste neden daha az oksijen var? Dayanak (1. paragraf): 'Hava basıncı daha düşük olduğu için; oksijenin havadaki oranı ise aynı kalır.'

title: Clocks in Carbon
text:
Radiocarbon dating, developed by the American chemist Willard Libby in the late 1940s, transformed archaeology by allowing organic remains to be dated independently of written records. The method relies on carbon-14, a radioactive form of carbon produced continuously in the upper atmosphere when cosmic rays strike nitrogen atoms. Living organisms take up carbon-14 along with ordinary carbon, through photosynthesis or by eating plants, so their tissues reflect the atmospheric ratio. Once an organism dies, however, no new carbon is absorbed, and the carbon-14 it contains decays at a known rate, halving roughly every 5,730 years. Measuring the remaining proportion therefore indicates how long ago death occurred.

Libby assumed that the atmospheric level of carbon-14 had been constant, but this later proved incorrect: it has varied with changes in solar activity and in the Earth's magnetic field. Raw radiocarbon ages must therefore be calibrated against records of known age, such as annual tree rings. Furthermore, because so little carbon-14 remains after about 50,000 years, the technique cannot be applied to older material, and samples must be protected from contamination by modern carbon, which can make them appear considerably younger.

title: What Teeth Remember
text:
Archaeologists have traditionally reconstructed ancient diets from animal bones, charred seeds and cooking vessels found at settlements. Such evidence reveals what was available at a site, but not necessarily what particular individuals ate. Increasingly, researchers are turning to a less obvious source: dental calculus, the hardened plaque that builds up on teeth when they are not cleaned.

As plaque mineralises during a person's lifetime, it traps tiny particles of food, such as starch grains and plant fragments, together with bacteria from the mouth. Because calculus is extremely durable, these remains can survive for thousands of years, protected inside a mineral shell. Analyses of calculus from Neanderthals, for example, have revealed traces of cooked plant foods, challenging the once common view that their diet consisted almost entirely of meat.

Calculus also preserves DNA and proteins. Researchers have identified milk proteins in the calculus of prehistoric herders, providing direct evidence of dairy consumption, and have tracked changes in oral bacteria associated with the adoption of farming. The method has limitations, however: not every food leaves recognisable traces, and the amount of calculus varies greatly between individuals, so the absence of evidence does not prove that a food was not eaten.

questions.q: According to the passage, traditional evidence such as animal bones and seeds ----.
options: cannot survive at settlements for thousands of years
has proved that the diet of Neanderthals consisted almost entirely of meat
shows what food was available at a site rather than who ate it
contains the DNA and proteins of particular individuals

questions.anlam: Soru: Hayvan kemikleri ve tohumlar gibi geleneksel kanıtlar hakkında ne söyleniyor? Dayanak (1. paragraf): 'Bir yerde ne bulunduğunu gösterir, ama belirli kişilerin ne yediğini göstermez.'

title: Spacing Out to Remember
text:
Students preparing for an exam often study a topic intensively in a single long session, a strategy commonly called cramming. Cramming can produce good results on a test the following day, but much of the material is forgotten soon afterwards. A large body of research shows that the same amount of study time is far more effective when it is spread over several sessions separated by intervals, a phenomenon known as the spacing effect.

The effect was first described in the 1880s by the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus, who tested his own memory for lists of nonsense syllables. Since then, it has been confirmed for many kinds of material, from vocabulary to motor skills, and in learners of all ages.

Why spacing helps is not entirely clear. One explanation is that, when some forgetting has occurred between sessions, recalling the information requires more effort, and this effort strengthens the memory. Another suggests that studying at different times links the material to a wider range of contexts, which later serve as retrieval cues. Interestingly, learners frequently judge massed study to be more effective, probably because information feels familiar when it has just been reviewed.

questions.q: According to the passage, cramming ----.

is more effective than spacing for learning motor skills

questions.explain: Metin 'can produce good results on a test the following day, but much of the material is forgotten soon afterwards' diyor. Şık bunu 'good short-term results ... followed by rapid forgetting' ile veriyor.
questions.anlam: Soru: Metne göre son dakika yüklenme (cramming) nasıl bir sonuç verir? Dayanak (1. paragraf): 'Ertesi günkü sınavda iyi sonuç verebilir ama malzemenin çoğu kısa sürede unutulur.'

title: Metals That Remember
text:
Most metals stay bent after they have been deformed. Shape-memory alloys, however, can return to their original shape when they are heated. The best-known example is nitinol, an alloy of nickel and titanium that was developed at a US naval laboratory in the early 1960s.

The secret lies in the arrangement of atoms. At low temperatures, the atoms of nitinol form a structure that can be bent easily without breaking the metal. When the alloy is warmed above a certain temperature, the atoms move back into their original, more rigid arrangement, and the part recovers its earlier shape. Engineers can choose this temperature by slightly changing the amount of nickel in the alloy.

Shape-memory alloys are now used in many fields. In medicine, thin nitinol tubes called stents are folded to a small size, pushed into a narrow blood vessel and then opened by body heat. Similar alloys are used in eyeglass frames that survive being sat on, and in small valves that open or close automatically when water reaches a certain temperature. Their main drawbacks are high cost and a limited life under repeated bending.

title: Batteries Without Lithium
text:
Lithium-ion batteries power almost every phone and electric car on the market. Lithium, however, is mined in only a few countries, and its price rose sharply when demand for electric vehicles grew. This has encouraged researchers to look again at an older idea: batteries that use sodium instead.

Sodium works in a similar way to lithium. During charging, sodium ions travel from one electrode to the other through a liquid electrolyte, and during use they move back, releasing energy. The great advantage of sodium is that it is extremely common, since it can be obtained from ordinary salt. Sodium-ion cells also perform better in freezing weather and can be stored safely with no charge at all, which simplifies transport.

The main weakness is weight. Sodium ions are larger and heavier than lithium ions, so a sodium battery stores less energy for the same mass. For this reason, experts do not expect sodium to replace lithium in long-range cars. Instead, the new cells are likely to be used in small city vehicles and in large stationary batteries that store solar and wind power, where low cost matters more than low weight.

title: Surviving the Impossible
text:
Tardigrades, tiny animals less than a millimetre long, are often described as the toughest creatures on Earth. They live in moss, soil and ocean sediments, and they normally need a thin film of water around them to remain active. What makes them remarkable is what happens when that water disappears.

As its surroundings dry out, a tardigrade pulls in its legs, loses almost all of its body water and curls into a dry, lifeless-looking form known as a tun. In this state its metabolism falls to less than 0.01 per cent of the normal rate. Tuns have survived temperatures close to absolute zero, years without water and even exposure to the vacuum of space. When water returns, the animal can become active again within hours.

For a long time it was assumed that tardigrades relied mainly on a sugar called trehalose, which protects the cells of some other dry-tolerant organisms. Many tardigrade species, however, produce little of it. Instead, researchers have identified unusual proteins that form a glass-like gel inside the cells as they dry, holding other molecules in place. Scientists hope that similar proteins might one day allow vaccines and medicines to be stored without refrigeration.

title: Why We Get a Fever
text:
A fever is a rise in body temperature above the normal level of about 37 °C. Many people see it as a problem that must be stopped as quickly as possible. In fact, a fever is usually part of the body's own defence against infection.

When bacteria or viruses enter the body, white blood cells release chemical messengers. These messengers travel to a small region of the brain called the hypothalamus, which acts like a thermostat. The hypothalamus then sets a higher target temperature, and the body responds by shivering and by reducing blood flow to the skin. This is why a person with a rising fever often feels cold.

A higher temperature helps the body in two ways. Many germs grow more slowly when they are warmer than normal, and some immune cells work faster at higher temperatures. For this reason, doctors do not always recommend lowering a mild fever in an otherwise healthy adult. A very high fever, however, can be dangerous, especially for babies and elderly people, and it should be treated by a doctor.

title: When Corals Turn White
text:
Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they support about a quarter of all marine species. The corals that build them are animals, but they depend on tiny algae living inside their tissues. The algae use sunlight to produce food, much of which they pass to the coral, and they also give the coral its colour.

This partnership is sensitive to heat. When the water stays only one or two degrees warmer than usual for several weeks, the algae begin to produce harmful chemicals, and the coral expels them. Without its algae, the coral loses its colour, a process known as bleaching. Bleached corals are not dead, but they are starving, and if the water does not cool down soon, many of them die.

Mass bleaching events were almost unknown before the 1980s. Since then, they have become more frequent as ocean temperatures have risen. Reefs need around ten years to recover from a severe event, but the gaps between events are becoming shorter. Scientists are therefore testing ways to help reefs, such as breeding corals that tolerate higher temperatures.

title: Zero Resistance
text:
In an ordinary copper wire, moving electrons constantly collide with vibrating atoms, and part of the electrical energy is lost as heat. In 1911, the Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes discovered that mercury cooled to about minus 269 °C loses its electrical resistance completely. A current started in a loop of such a superconductor can, in principle, flow for years without any power supply.

Superconductors have another striking property: they push magnetic fields out of their interior. A small magnet placed above a cooled superconductor therefore floats in the air. This effect, together with the ability to carry very large currents, makes superconductors ideal for the powerful electromagnets in medical scanners and particle accelerators.

The main obstacle to wider use is the need for extreme cold. Early superconductors had to be cooled with liquid helium, which is expensive and scarce. In 1986, researchers found ceramic materials that become superconducting at higher temperatures, cold enough to be reached with cheap liquid nitrogen. These ceramics, however, are brittle and difficult to form into wires. A material that superconducts at room temperature would transform power grids, but despite many claims, none has yet been confirmed.

title: Cleaning the Exhaust
text:
When petrol burns in a car engine, it produces not only carbon dioxide and water but also several harmful gases. These include carbon monoxide, which is poisonous, unburnt fuel and nitrogen oxides, which help to form smog. Since the 1970s, most new cars have been fitted with a device called a catalytic converter to reduce these pollutants.

A catalytic converter is a metal box in the exhaust pipe. Inside it there is a ceramic block with thousands of tiny channels, coated with small amounts of precious metals such as platinum and rhodium. These metals act as catalysts: they speed up chemical reactions without being used up themselves. As the hot exhaust gases pass through the channels, carbon monoxide and unburnt fuel are changed into carbon dioxide and water, while nitrogen oxides are turned back into nitrogen.

Catalytic converters work well only when they are hot, so most pollution from modern cars is produced in the first few minutes after a cold start. The precious metals inside them are also valuable, and in some cities thieves have begun to steal converters from parked cars.

title: Fixing Errors Automatically
text:
Whenever data is sent over a network or stored on a disc, some bits may be changed by electrical noise, scratches or radiation. A single wrong bit can turn a number into a different number or make a file impossible to open. Engineers therefore add extra bits to the data, which allow errors to be detected and often corrected.

The simplest method is the parity bit. A sender counts the number of ones in a group of bits and adds one more bit so that the total is always even. If the receiver finds an odd total, it knows that something has gone wrong. A parity bit, however, cannot show which bit is wrong, and it fails if two bits change at the same time.

More advanced codes, first developed by Richard Hamming in 1950, use several check bits arranged so that the position of a wrong bit can be calculated and repaired automatically. Similar ideas protect QR codes, which can still be read when part of the pattern is dirty or torn, and they allow space probes billions of kilometres away to send clear images back to Earth.

title: When the Ground Turns to Liquid
text:
During strong earthquakes, buildings sometimes tilt or sink even though their walls remain undamaged. The cause is often not the shaking itself but a process called soil liquefaction, in which solid ground temporarily behaves like a thick liquid.

Liquefaction occurs mainly in loose, sandy soils that are saturated with water, such as those found near rivers, coasts and reclaimed land. Normally, the sand grains touch one another, and friction between them allows the soil to carry the weight of buildings. When an earthquake shakes the ground, the grains try to settle into a tighter arrangement. Because the water between them cannot escape quickly enough, its pressure rises until the grains are no longer pressed together. At that moment the soil loses most of its strength, and heavy structures sink while light ones, such as buried tanks, may float upwards.

Engineers cannot prevent earthquakes, but they can reduce this risk. Common methods include compacting loose sand with heavy vibrating machines, installing drains that let water escape during shaking, and supporting buildings on deep piles that reach firmer layers. Mapping areas prone to liquefaction also helps planners decide where new buildings should not be placed.

title: Trading Speed for Force
text:
Gears are toothed wheels that pass motion from one shaft to another. They are found in clocks, bicycles, washing machines and car gearboxes, and they have been used for more than two thousand years. Their main job is not to create power but to change the balance between speed and turning force, which engineers call torque.

When a small gear drives a larger one, the larger gear turns more slowly but with greater torque. If the large gear has three times as many teeth as the small one, it turns at one third of the speed but with about three times the force. This is why a cyclist climbing a steep hill chooses a low gear: the pedals turn easily, although the bicycle moves slowly. When the small gear is driven by the large one, the opposite happens, and speed increases while torque falls.

No gear system is perfect. Friction between the teeth turns a small part of the energy into heat and noise, so the output power is always slightly less than the input. For this reason, gears are carefully shaped and usually kept in oil.

questions.q: According to the passage, when a small gear drives a larger one, the larger gear ----.

title: Concrete That Repairs Itself
text:
Concrete is the most widely used building material in the world, but it has a common weakness: it cracks. Small cracks are not dangerous in themselves, yet they allow water and salts to reach the steel bars inside, which then begin to corrode. Repairing such damage on bridges and tunnels is slow and expensive.

One promising solution is self-healing concrete. In one version, developed in the Netherlands, the concrete mix contains spores of special bacteria together with a food source such as calcium lactate. The spores can remain inactive inside the hard concrete for many years. When a crack forms and water enters, they wake up, feed and produce limestone, which gradually fills the gap. Cracks up to about one millimetre wide can be sealed in this way within a few weeks.

Self-healing concrete currently costs considerably more than ordinary concrete, so it is mainly being tested in structures that are hard to reach, such as underground tanks and tunnel walls. Supporters argue that the higher initial price may be repaid by lower maintenance costs over the life of a structure.

title: The Cost of Green Hydrogen
text:
Hydrogen is often presented as the fuel of the future, because burning it produces only water. Almost all hydrogen made today, however, comes from natural gas, in a process that releases large amounts of carbon dioxide. So-called green hydrogen is produced instead by electrolysis, in which an electric current splits water into hydrogen and oxygen, using electricity from renewable sources.

The difficulty lies in energy losses. Modern electrolysers convert only about 70 per cent of the electrical energy they use into chemical energy stored in hydrogen. Further energy is needed to compress or cool the gas for storage, and when hydrogen is turned back into electricity in a fuel cell, roughly half of the remaining energy is lost again. As a result, a car running on green hydrogen needs about three times as much renewable electricity per kilometre as a battery car.

For this reason, many energy experts argue that green hydrogen should be reserved for uses where batteries and direct electricity are impractical. These include steelmaking, where hydrogen can replace coal in removing oxygen from iron ore, the production of fertilisers, and possibly long-distance shipping and aviation.

title: The Body's Inner Clock
text:
Most living things, from bacteria to humans, have an internal clock that follows a cycle of about 24 hours. This cycle, called the circadian rhythm, controls when we feel sleepy, when our body temperature rises and falls, and when certain hormones are released.

In humans, the master clock is a small group of nerve cells in the brain. It keeps time on its own, but it is adjusted every day by light entering the eyes. Morning light, in particular, tells the clock that the day has begun. In the evening, as light fades, the brain releases a hormone called melatonin, which helps to prepare the body for sleep.

Problems arise when daily life does not match the inner clock. People who fly across several time zones suffer from jet lag, feeling tired during the day and awake at night until their clock adjusts. Night-shift workers face a similar but longer-lasting problem, and studies have linked years of shift work with a higher risk of some illnesses. Bright screens late in the evening may also delay the clock by reducing the release of melatonin.

title: Antibiotics and the Gut
text:
The human gut contains trillions of bacteria belonging to hundreds of species. Far from being harmful, most of them help us: they break down fibre that our own enzymes cannot digest, produce certain vitamins and train the immune system. A healthy gut community also makes it harder for dangerous bacteria to settle.

Antibiotics save millions of lives, but they do not only kill the bacteria causing an infection. Many of them also destroy large numbers of helpful gut bacteria. After a typical course of treatment, most species return within a few weeks, yet studies have found that some may still be missing months later. During this period, a harmful bacterium called Clostridioides difficile can multiply in the weakened community and cause severe diarrhoea, especially in elderly hospital patients.

Doctors therefore try to prescribe antibiotics only when they are truly needed and to choose drugs that act on as few species as possible. For patients with repeated C. difficile infections, an unusual treatment has proved highly effective: transferring gut bacteria from a healthy donor. This restores a diverse community that can push out the harmful species.

title: Dead Zones in the Sea
text:
Every summer, an area of the Gulf of Mexico several thousand square kilometres in size becomes almost empty of fish and shrimp. Similar so-called dead zones have been reported in more than 400 coastal regions worldwide, from the Baltic Sea to the coasts of China. Their main cause lies far inland, on farmland.

Fertilisers containing nitrogen and phosphorus are spread on fields to increase crop yields, but a large share is washed into rivers by rain. When this nutrient-rich water reaches the sea, it feeds huge blooms of algae near the surface. As the algae die, they sink and are broken down by bacteria, which consume dissolved oxygen in the process. In calm summer weather, warm fresh water lies on top of colder salt water and prevents oxygen from the air from mixing downwards. Near the bottom, oxygen levels fall so low that animals must flee or die.

Dead zones can recover. When fertiliser use around the Black Sea fell sharply in the 1990s for economic reasons, the dead zone there shrank considerably. Farmers can reduce runoff by applying fertiliser more precisely and by planting strips of vegetation along rivers.

title: Why the Sky Is Blue
text:
Sunlight looks white, but it is actually a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow. Each colour has a different wavelength: red light has the longest waves, and blue and violet light have the shortest. When sunlight enters the atmosphere, it meets countless tiny molecules of nitrogen and oxygen.

These molecules scatter light, that is, they send it off in new directions. Importantly, they scatter short wavelengths much more strongly than long ones. Blue light is therefore spread across the whole sky, and whichever direction we look, some of it reaches our eyes. Violet light is scattered even more, but the Sun produces less of it, and our eyes are less sensitive to it, so the sky appears blue rather than violet.

The same effect explains red sunsets. When the Sun is low, its light must travel through a much thicker layer of air before reaching us. By then, most of the blue light has been scattered away to the sides, and mainly orange and red light remains. On the Moon, which has no atmosphere, there is no scattering, and the sky looks black even during the day.

title: Capturing Carbon from Chimneys
text:
Power stations and cement works release enormous amounts of carbon dioxide through their chimneys. One way to reduce these emissions is carbon capture: removing the gas from the exhaust before it enters the atmosphere and storing it underground.

The most developed method uses liquids called amines, which are related to ammonia. The exhaust gas is passed upwards through a tall tower while the amine solution flows downwards. Carbon dioxide reacts with the amine and is held in the liquid, while the other gases, mainly nitrogen, pass out of the top. The liquid is then pumped to a second tower and heated to about 120 °C. At this temperature, the reaction reverses, pure carbon dioxide is released and collected, and the amine can be used again.

The process works, but it is costly. Heating the solution consumes a large part of the energy produced by a power station, often about a quarter, and amines slowly break down and must be replaced. Researchers are therefore testing solid materials with many tiny pores that capture carbon dioxide and release it at lower temperatures.

title: Bits That Are Both
text:
An ordinary computer stores information as bits, each of which is either 0 or 1. A quantum computer uses qubits, which can exist in a combination of both states at once until they are measured. When several qubits are linked through a phenomenon called entanglement, the number of states they represent together doubles with every qubit added. In principle, this allows certain calculations to explore a vast number of possibilities in parallel.

It is a common misunderstanding, however, that quantum computers will simply be faster at everything. Their advantage applies only to particular problems, such as simulating molecules for drug design or factoring very large numbers, which is the basis of much of today's internet encryption. For everyday tasks like word processing, an ordinary computer will remain more practical.

The greatest technical challenge is fragility. Qubits lose their quantum state when disturbed by heat, vibration or stray electromagnetic fields, a problem known as decoherence. Most current machines must therefore be cooled to a fraction of a degree above absolute zero. Because errors accumulate quickly, many physical qubits may be needed to create a single reliable one, and machines large enough to break encryption are probably still years away.

title: Rivers of Ice
text:
A glacier is a large mass of ice that moves slowly over land. Glaciers form in places where more snow falls in winter than melts in summer. Year after year, the snow builds up and is pressed into dense ice by the weight of the layers above. When the ice becomes thick enough, it begins to flow downhill under its own weight, usually by only a few metres a year, although some glaciers move much faster.

As they move, glaciers act like giant files. Rocks frozen into the bottom of the ice scrape the ground below and break off pieces of bedrock. Over thousands of years, this process turns narrow river valleys, which are usually V-shaped, into wide valleys with a U-shaped cross-section. Many famous landscapes, such as the fjords of Norway, were shaped in this way during past ice ages.

Today, most glaciers around the world are shrinking as temperatures rise. This matters not only for the landscape: in regions such as the Andes and the Himalayas, millions of people depend on meltwater from glaciers for drinking water and farming during the dry season.

title: Listening to Bearings
text:
Rolling bearings support rotating shafts in almost every machine, from small electric motors to the huge rolls of steel mills. When a bearing fails unexpectedly, a production line may stop for hours or days. For this reason, many plants no longer replace bearings at fixed intervals but monitor their condition while the machines are running.

The most common method is vibration analysis. Small sensors called accelerometers are mounted on the bearing housing and record its vibration. A healthy bearing produces a low, fairly even signal. When a tiny crack or pit appears on one of the rings or rolling elements, each roller strikes the damaged spot as it passes, creating a short impact. Because the geometry and speed of the bearing are known, engineers can calculate at what frequency these impacts should repeat, and so identify which part is damaged.

Other signs can support the diagnosis. A rise in temperature often indicates poor lubrication, while metal particles in the oil show that wear is taking place. By combining these signals, maintenance teams can plan a replacement during a scheduled stop, often weeks before the bearing would actually fail.

title: Failure Without Overload
text:
A steel part can break under a load that is far below its tensile strength if that load is applied and removed many thousands of times. This type of failure, called fatigue, is responsible for a large proportion of mechanical failures in service, including famous accidents involving early jet airliners in the 1950s.

Fatigue usually begins at a point where stress is concentrated, such as a sharp corner, a hole or a scratch on the surface. With each loading cycle, a microscopic crack grows a little further. For most of the part's life the crack remains too small to see, and the part shows no outward sign of damage. Finally, the remaining cross-section becomes too small to carry the load, and the part fractures suddenly.

Designers fight fatigue in several ways. They avoid sharp changes in shape, polish critical surfaces and use processes such as shot peening, which places the surface layer under compression and makes it harder for cracks to open. Since fatigue strength cannot be predicted exactly, parts are also inspected regularly.

title: Moving Heat Uphill
text:
Heat naturally flows from warm places to cold ones. A heat pump uses electricity to move it the other way: from the cold air or ground outside into a warm house. A refrigerator works on the same principle, taking heat out of the food compartment and releasing it into the kitchen.

Inside a heat pump, a special liquid called a refrigerant circulates in a closed loop. Outside the house, it evaporates at a low temperature and absorbs heat from the air, even on cold days. A compressor then squeezes the gas, which raises its temperature sharply. Indoors, the hot gas condenses back into a liquid and gives its heat to the water or air of the heating system.

The main advantage is efficiency. For every unit of electricity it uses, a typical heat pump delivers three or four units of heat, because most of the energy comes from outside. An electric heater, by contrast, delivers only one. Heat pumps are, however, more expensive to install than gas boilers, and they work best in well-insulated buildings.

title: Editing Genes with Precision
text:
For decades, changing the genes of a living organism was slow, expensive and imprecise. This changed in 2012, when Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed that a bacterial defence system known as CRISPR could be turned into a simple tool for cutting DNA at a chosen place.

In nature, bacteria use CRISPR to recognise and destroy the DNA of viruses that have attacked them before. The tool consists of two parts: a short piece of guide RNA, which matches the target sequence, and an enzyme called Cas9, which cuts both strands of the DNA there. When the cell repairs the cut, a gene can be switched off, or a new piece of DNA can be inserted.

CRISPR has spread rapidly through laboratories because it is cheap and easy to use. In 2023, the first CRISPR-based treatment was approved for sickle cell disease, an inherited blood disorder. The technique also raises ethical concerns, particularly about changing human embryos, since such changes would be passed on to future generations.

options: is the enzyme, called Cas9, that cuts both strands of the DNA at the target

title: Targeted Medicines from the Immune System
text:
Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins produced by the immune system. Each one recognises a single target, such as a particular molecule on the surface of a virus, and attaches to it. In 1975, Georges Köhler and César Milstein found a way to produce large quantities of identical antibodies in the laboratory, so-called monoclonal antibodies.

These molecules have become some of the most important medicines of recent decades. Because they bind only to their chosen target, they can act on diseased cells while largely sparing healthy ones. Some mark cancer cells so that the patient's own immune system destroys them; others block signals that drive inflammation in diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis.

Monoclonal antibodies do, however, have drawbacks. Being large proteins, they would be digested in the stomach, so they cannot be taken as tablets and must be injected or infused. They are also costly to manufacture, which makes treatment expensive for health systems. Early versions made in mice sometimes caused allergic reactions, a problem largely solved by modern antibodies, which are almost entirely human.

title: Nature's Water Filters
text:
Wetlands such as marshes and swamps were once seen as useless land, and many were drained to make room for farms and cities. Scientists now know that they provide valuable services, one of the most important being the cleaning of water.

As water flows slowly through a wetland, mud and other particles settle to the bottom. Plants take up nitrogen and phosphorus, nutrients that would otherwise pollute rivers and lakes. Bacteria living around the roots break down many harmful substances, and some even turn nitrogen compounds into harmless nitrogen gas. In this way, a healthy wetland can remove a large part of the pollution from farm runoff before it reaches open water.

Wetlands also store water during heavy rain and release it slowly, which reduces flooding downstream. Because of these benefits, some towns have built artificial wetlands to treat their wastewater. These systems use little energy and are cheaper to run than conventional treatment plants, although they need much more land.

title: Silence from Sound
text:
Sound travels through air as a wave of tiny pressure changes. When two sound waves meet, their effects add together. If the high-pressure parts of one wave meet the high-pressure parts of another, the sound becomes louder. If, however, the high-pressure parts of one wave meet the low-pressure parts of another, the two can cancel each other out. This effect is called destructive interference.

Noise-cancelling headphones use this principle. A small microphone on the outside of each ear cup picks up the surrounding noise. An electronic circuit then produces an opposite wave, and the speaker plays it together with the music. When the two waves meet inside the ear cup, much of the noise disappears.

The system works best for steady, low-pitched sounds, such as the hum of an aircraft engine, because these waves are long and change slowly enough for the electronics to follow. Sudden or high-pitched sounds, like voices or a dog barking, are harder to cancel. For this reason, headphones also rely on soft padding that physically blocks higher frequencies.

questions.explain: Metin 'A small microphone on the outside of each ear cup picks up the surrounding noise' diyor.

title: Left-Handed and Right-Handed Molecules
text:
Many molecules exist in two forms that contain exactly the same atoms joined in the same order but are mirror images of each other, like a left and a right hand. Such molecules are called chiral. The two forms, known as enantiomers, have identical boiling points and most other physical properties, yet they can behave very differently in the body.

The reason is that the receptors and enzymes in our cells are themselves chiral. Just as a left hand fits only a left glove, an enzyme may interact strongly with one enantiomer and hardly at all with the other. The two forms of the molecule carvone, for example, smell of spearmint and of caraway respectively.

In medicine, the difference can be critical. In the late 1950s, the drug thalidomide was sold as a mixture of both forms to ease morning sickness in pregnant women. One form was later linked to severe birth defects, although the body can convert one form into the other. Since then, regulators have required companies to test each enantiomer separately, and many modern drugs are produced as a single form.

title: Making Files Smaller
text:
Every photo, song and document on a computer is stored as a long series of bits. Many files contain patterns and repetitions, and compression programs take advantage of them to store the same information in less space.

There are two main types of compression. Lossless compression allows the original file to be rebuilt exactly. A simple example is replacing a row of one hundred identical white pixels with a short instruction meaning "one hundred white pixels". Text documents and computer programs must always be compressed in this way, since changing even a single character could make them useless.

Lossy compression, by contrast, throws away some information permanently. Formats such as JPEG for images and MP3 for music remove details that people are unlikely to notice, such as very small changes in colour or very quiet sounds hidden behind loud ones. As a result, files can be made ten times smaller or more. If a lossy file is compressed and saved again and again, however, the quality gradually becomes worse.

title: Seconds of Warning
text:
Earthquakes cannot yet be predicted days or hours in advance, but it is possible to warn people a few seconds before strong shaking arrives. This is the aim of earthquake early warning systems, which now operate in Japan, Mexico, parts of the United States and several other countries.

The systems rely on the fact that an earthquake sends out two main kinds of waves. The first, called P-waves, travel faster but usually cause little damage. The slower S-waves and surface waves that follow produce most of the destructive shaking. A network of sensors detects the first P-waves near the source, and computers quickly estimate the location and size of the earthquake. A warning is then sent by mobile phone, radio and television to areas that the stronger waves have not yet reached.

The warning time depends on distance. People very close to the source may receive no warning at all, while those a hundred kilometres away may have twenty seconds or more. Even a few seconds, however, are enough to stop trains, open fire station doors and allow people to take cover under a table.

title: A Thin Film of Oil
text:
In a well-lubricated journal bearing, the rotating shaft never actually touches the bearing surface. Instead, it rides on a thin film of oil, often only a few thousandths of a millimetre thick. This condition, called hydrodynamic lubrication, explains why such bearings in turbines can run for decades with very little wear.

The film is created by the motion itself. Because the shaft sits slightly off-centre, the gap between shaft and bearing narrows on one side. As the rotating shaft drags oil into this narrowing wedge, pressure builds up in the oil and lifts the shaft. The faster the shaft turns and the thicker the oil, the higher the pressure and the thicker the film.

The weakest moments are therefore starting and stopping. At low speeds the film is too thin to separate the surfaces, and metal rubs against metal. To reduce this damage, large machines often use a separate pump that forces oil into the bearing under high pressure before the shaft begins to turn. Overheating is another danger, since hot oil becomes thinner and may no longer support the load.
